subject: Thermodynamics + Applied Thermodynamics
summary: a full revision of Thermodynamics (pure substances, ideal-gas entropy, the second law with several reservoirs, the third law, throttling) and Applied Thermodynamics (Rankine and binary cycles, gas-turbine behaviour, multi-stage compressors, SI and CI engine performance, psychrometry, vapour-compression refrigeration and compounded steam turbines)

questions.text: The third law of thermodynamics states that
opts: the entropy of every substance is zero at 0 K
the entropy of a pure, perfectly crystalline substance is zero at absolute zero
the entropy of an isolated system can never decrease
absolute zero can be reached in a finite number of steps
questions.ans: (B) the entropy of a pure, perfectly crystalline substance is zero at absolute zero
solution: Concept: The third law fixes the zero of entropy: S → 0 as T → 0 for a pure substance in perfect crystalline equilibrium (Planck statement).
Glasses, mixtures and imperfect crystals keep a residual entropy at 0 K, so option A is too broad.
Option C is the increase-of-entropy principle (second law); the third law in fact implies that 0 K cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.
Answer: (B)
Exam tip: The third law is what makes absolute entropy values (used in combustion and chemical equilibrium) possible.

questions.text: A rigid tank contains dry saturated steam at 300 kPa (v<sub>g</sub> = 0.6058 m³/kg). It is cooled until the pressure falls to 100 kPa, where v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001043 m³/kg and v<sub>g</sub> = 1.6941 m³/kg. The dryness fraction at the final state (round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: In a rigid closed tank the mass and the volume are fixed, so the specific volume stays constant during cooling.
v<sub>2</sub> = v<sub>1</sub> = 0.6058 m³/kg, which lies between v<sub>f</sub> and v<sub>g</sub> at 100 kPa, so the steam is wet.
Exam tip: On a T–v diagram a rigid-tank process is a vertical line; cooling dry steam drops it into the wet region.

questions.text: Air (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K) is compressed from 100 kPa, 300 K to 500 kPa, 450 K. The change in its specific entropy is about
solution: Concept: For an ideal gas, Δs = cp ln(T2/T1) − R ln(p2/p1).
Exam tip: A negative Δs is allowed here: the compressor is not adiabatic in this data (heat leaves the air), so entropy can fall.

questions.text: A reversible engine receives 3000 kJ from a reservoir at 1000 K, exchanges heat with two other reservoirs at 600 K and 300 K, and produces 1500 kJ of work, as shown. The heat rejected to the 300 K reservoir (in kJ) is ______
solution: Concept: For a reversible engine both laws apply as equalities: Σ Q = W and Σ Q/T = 0 (Clausius).
First law: Q<sub>2</sub> + Q<sub>3</sub> = 3000 − 1500 = 1500 kJ (heat rejected at 600 K and 300 K)
Q2 = 1200 kJ and Q3 = 300 kJ (both positive, so both are rejections, as assumed)
Exam tip: If a solution gives a negative Q, that reservoir is actually supplying heat; the sign tells you the direction.

questions.text: In a mercury–steam binary vapour cycle, mercury is used as the working fluid of the topping cycle mainly because
opts: its critical temperature is low
its saturation pressure is low even at high temperatures, so heat can be added at a high temperature without very high pressures
its latent heat of vaporisation is very large
it does not need a condenser
questions.ans: (B) its saturation pressure is low even at high temperatures, so heat can be added at a high temperature without very high pressures
solution: Concept: Rankine efficiency rises with the mean temperature of heat addition, but steam needs enormous pressures to boil at high temperatures.
Mercury boils at about 500 °C at only about 10 bar, so the topping cycle adds heat at a high temperature at a modest pressure.
Its condenser rejects heat to boil water for the steam (bottoming) cycle. Its latent heat is actually small, so a large mass of mercury must circulate.
Answer: (B)
Exam tip: Binary cycles try to make the overall cycle look like a Carnot cycle by stacking fluids that suit different temperature ranges.

questions.text: In an ideal Rankine cycle, steam enters the turbine at 6 MPa and 500 °C (h = 3423.1 kJ/kg, s = 6.8826 kJ/kg·K) and the condenser pressure is 10 kPa. At 10 kPa: h<sub>f</sub> = 191.81 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2392.1 kJ/kg, s<sub>f</sub> = 0.6492 kJ/kg·K, s<sub>fg</sub> = 7.4996 kJ/kg·K and v<sub>f</sub> = 0.00101 m³/kg. The thermal efficiency of the cycle (in %, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Ideal Rankine: isentropic turbine and pump; η = (WT − WP)/Qin (cycle shown below).
Exam tip: The exhaust dryness here is only 0.83; below about 0.88 blade erosion becomes a concern, which is why reheat is used.

questions.text: When the ambient (compressor inlet) temperature of a simple gas turbine plant with real (non-isentropic) compressor and turbine rises on a hot day, with the same pressure ratio and turbine inlet temperature,
opts: the net output and the thermal efficiency both increase
the net output increases but the thermal efficiency falls
the net output and the thermal efficiency both fall
the net output falls but the thermal efficiency is unaffected
questions.ans: (C) the net output and the thermal efficiency both fall
solution: Concept: Compressor work per kg is proportional to the inlet temperature, while the turbine work depends on the (unchanged) turbine inlet temperature.
A hotter intake raises the compressor work and lowers the air density, so the mass flow falls: the net output drops.
With real (non-ideal) machines the efficiency also falls, because the compressor work rises while the heat added (T<sub>3</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>) shrinks less than the net work.
Answer: (C)
Exam tip: This is why inlet-air cooling (evaporative or chiller) is used on gas turbines in hot climates.

questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT an advantage of multi-stage compression with intercooling over single-stage compression to the same delivery pressure?
opts: Less work input per kg of air
Higher volumetric efficiency of the first stage
Lower delivery temperature in each stage
Fewer moving parts and a simpler machine
questions.ans: (D) Fewer moving parts and a simpler machine
solution: Concept: Staging with intercooling brings the compression closer to isothermal and reduces the pressure ratio per stage.
Work input falls (shaded area saved on the p–V diagram), each stage delivers cooler air, and the lower stage pressure ratio raises the volumetric efficiency.
The price is more cylinders, valves and an intercooler: the machine becomes more complex.
Answer: (D)
Exam tip: Optimum intermediate pressure for two stages is √(p1p3), which gives equal work in both stages.

questions.text: A four-stroke SI engine of 2.0 L displacement runs at 3000 rpm with a volumetric efficiency of 85 % (based on an air density of 1.18 kg/m³). The air–fuel ratio is 14.7, the calorific value of the fuel is 44 000 kJ/kg and the brake thermal efficiency is 30 %. The brake power (in kW, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Air flow = ηv ρa Vs (N/2) for a four-stroke engine; fuel flow = air flow/(A/F); BP = ηbth ṁf CV.
Exam tip: In a four-stroke engine each cylinder breathes once every two revolutions; forgetting N/2 doubles the answer.

questions.text: The power output of an SI engine is controlled by ____, whereas that of a CI engine is controlled by ____.
opts: throttling the air–fuel mixture (quantity governing); varying the fuel quantity injected with unthrottled air (quality governing)
varying the fuel quantity at a fixed air flow (quality governing); throttling the mixture (quantity governing)
advancing the spark; retarding the injection
changing the compression ratio; changing the injection pressure
questions.ans: (A) throttling the air–fuel mixture (quantity governing); varying the fuel quantity injected with unthrottled air (quality governing)
solution: Concept: An SI engine must burn a near-stoichiometric mixture for reliable flame propagation, so it is throttled: less mixture, same ratio (quantity governing).
A CI engine draws unthrottled air and the load is set by how much fuel is injected, so the A/F ratio varies (quality governing).
Throttling losses (pumping work) are one reason SI engines are less efficient at part load.
Answer: (A)
Exam tip: 'Quantity' and 'quality' refer to the mixture: its amount (SI) or its strength (CI).

questions.text: Moist air at 25 °C and a total pressure of 101.325 kPa has a specific humidity of 0.012 kg/kg of dry air. The saturation pressure of water at 25 °C is 3.169 kPa. The degree of saturation of the air (round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Degree of saturation μ = ω/ωs, where ωs is the specific humidity of saturated air at the same temperature and total pressure.
For comparison, p<sub>v</sub> = ωp/(0.622 + ω) = 1.918 kPa, so φ = 1.918/3.169 = 0.605: μ is slightly smaller than φ.
Exam tip: μ = φ(p − ps)/(p − pv); the two are nearly equal at room conditions and both equal 1 for saturated air.

questions.text: In a vapour-compression refrigerator, the condenser temperature rises (on a hot day) while the evaporator temperature stays the same. Then
opts: the refrigerating effect per kg increases and the COP increases
the refrigerating effect per kg is unchanged but the COP decreases
the refrigerating effect per kg and the COP both decrease, and the compressor work per kg increases
the compressor work per kg decreases and the COP increases
questions.ans: (C) the refrigerating effect per kg and the COP both decrease, and the compressor work per kg increases
solution: Concept: On the p–h diagram, a higher condensing pressure moves the saturated-liquid point (and the throttled state) to a higher enthalpy, and lengthens the compression line.
Refrigerating effect h<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>4</sub> falls because h<sub>4</sub> = h<sub>3</sub> rises; compressor work h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>1</sub> rises.
So COP = (h<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>4</sub>)/(h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>1</sub>) falls on both counts.
Answer: (C)
Exam tip: Keep condensers clean and well ventilated: every degree of extra condensing temperature costs roughly 2–3 % in COP.

questions.text: A room is kept at 25 °C. Its sensible heat load is 20 kW, and conditioned air is supplied at 14 °C. Taking the humid specific heat of the supply air as 1.022 kJ/kg·K (per kg of dry air), the required supply air flow (in kg of dry air per second, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: The supply air absorbs the room sensible heat as it warms from the supply temperature to the room temperature: RSH = ṁa cpm (troom − tsupply).
ṁa = 1.78 kg/s
Exam tip: The latent load does not enter this sizing; it fixes how dry the supply air must be (the RSHF line on the chart).

questions.text: A velocity-compounded (Curtis) impulse stage has two rows of moving blades. Steam leaves the nozzle at 800 m/s at 16° to the plane of the wheel. With symmetrical, frictionless blades, the blade speed for maximum diagram efficiency (in m/s, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: For an impulse stage with n rows of moving blades (symmetrical, frictionless), the optimum blade-speed ratio is u/V1 = cos α/(2n) and the maximum diagram efficiency is cos²α.
u = 0.2403 × 800 = 192.3 m/s (maximum diagram efficiency cos²16° = 92.4 %)
Exam tip: Curtis stages handle a large enthalpy drop at a low blade speed, but their actual efficiency falls quickly as rows are added.

questions.text: When wet steam at a high pressure is throttled to a low pressure (for example in a throttling calorimeter), its
opts: enthalpy stays the same and its dryness fraction increases (it may become superheated)
enthalpy and dryness fraction both stay the same
entropy stays the same and its dryness fraction decreases
enthalpy decreases and its temperature stays the same
questions.ans: (A) enthalpy stays the same and its dryness fraction increases (it may become superheated)
solution: Concept: Throttling is adiabatic with no work and negligible KE change, so h1 = h2; it is irreversible, so entropy rises.
At the lower pressure h<sub>f</sub> is much smaller, so the same enthalpy corresponds to a larger dryness fraction; if h exceeds h<sub>g</sub> at the low pressure, the steam becomes superheated.
On the h–s (Mollier) chart throttling is a horizontal line moving to the right.
Answer: (A)
Exam tip: A throttling calorimeter works only for nearly dry steam (x above about 0.95); wetter steam needs a separating calorimeter first.
